issues.issue: The clause turns on "the Parties", a capitalised term defined only in the separate Separation Agreement and never in this Agreement, and confers beneficiary status on Parent without saying which rights Parent may enforce. The extent of Parent's standing is unclear.

Michigan law is chosen, but the employer and payor is an Indian company employing an India-resident under Section 2.1, and Section 8.2(d) requires him to reside in India. Whether Michigan law can govern the India employment relationship is arguable.
"Disparage" is undefined and the obligation runs "thereafter" without end, so its boundary against truthful or legally required statements cannot be fixed. The sentence also ends without punctuation.

This imposes a perpetual mutual non-disparagement duty, while paragraph 3 of the attached Separation Agreement limits the Employee's duty to the period "[f]or so long as Employee holds Restricted Stock Units" and carves out statements to the Board. The two cannot both measure the same duty.

"May be brought against any of parties in the courts of the State of Michigan" is permissive in form yet coupled with consent to jurisdiction and a venue waiver, so whether the clause is exclusive or merely consensual is genuinely contestable. That is the classic mandatory-versus-permissive forum question.
The party block is a blank form — the Employee's name is missing — so the instrument as attached identifies no releasor. It is a form defect rather than a substantive ambiguity.
The recital breaks off with a blank where the Employment Agreement date should appear, leaving the released agreement unidentified on the face of the form. The sentence is incomplete.
The recital ends with a blank effective date of termination, which is the date the release period in paragraph 1 is measured to. As drafted it states nothing.

This recital says only that the Employee was given the "opportunity" to consult counsel, while operative paragraph 8 states that he was advised to and "did so". The recital and the operative acknowledgment do not match.

The release sweeps "any and all" claims "known or unknown" through a long enumerated statute list introduced by "including, but not limited to", then carves out only claims "to compel the payment of amounts due to Employee as provided in the Employment Agreement". Both the reach of the catch-all and the width of that single carve-out are open to construction.

The carve-out preserves claims for amounts due under the Employment Agreement, yet paragraph 19 releases the Company from "all of its remaining obligations" if the Employee breaches, and Section 8.4 conditions severance on this very release. The interlocking conditions are not fully reconciled.

The defined bundle "Company Information and Property" ends with the catch-all "all other assets, materials and information of any kind or nature, belonging or pertaining to Company", whose reach against the enumerated items is uncertain. "Pertaining to" has no boundary.

The Employee's obligation runs only "[f]or so long as Employee holds Restricted Stock Units", a term used nowhere else in this instrument or the Employment Agreement, yet the same sentence says he "shall never" disparage. The duration is both undefined and self-contradictory.

The Company's counter-promise addresses "the circumstances of Employee's resignation", although the release is drafted for any termination, and Section 9.13 of the Employment Agreement imposes an unconditional mutual duty. The two non-disparagement regimes differ in scope and duration.

The paragraph is a sentence fragment — "To never seek or accept employment with Company" has no subject or operative verb — so it is unclear who promises what. The grammatical defect goes to whether any obligation was created.

This preserves the Employment Agreement's confidentiality, proprietary-rights and noncompete obligations, but paragraph 15 says the release "contains the entire agreement between Employee and Company regarding the matters set forth herein". The interaction of the two is workable but not seamless.

"A reasonable amount of the Employee's time" and "reasonable notice" set no limit on the cooperation demanded, and reimbursement is for "lost wages" without a rate. The obligation's outer bound cannot be applied.

The revocation notice must be sent or delivered to addresses that are left blank in the form, so the prescribed method of revocation cannot be performed as written. Whether a revocation otherwise communicated is effective would have to be construed.

This paragraph says the Release "is not effective until this revocation period has expired", while paragraph 11 makes the Company's obligations contingent on the Employee also giving written confirmation that he did not revoke. The two conditions to effectiveness differ.

"The Company's obligations" is not identified — it may mean only severance or every obligation in the Release — and the required "written confirmation" has no deadline or form. The condition precedent is imprecise.

The Company may disclose the terms "only for legitimate business purposes", an undefined standard that gives the Company a broad and unmeasurable exception to a confidentiality promise binding the Employee absolutely. The asymmetry invites construction against the drafter.
"Regarding the matters set forth herein" limits the integration to unstated subject matter, leaving unclear what prior understandings survive. The qualifier does the work but is not defined.

This paragraph directs judicial reformation of any invalid provision, while Section 9.2 of the Employment Agreement leaves an invalid provision simply severed. The two savings clauses in the same package operate differently.

The forfeiture is of the Company's obligations "under the Severance Agreement", a term used nowhere else — this instrument is defined as the "Release" and the pay obligation sits in Section 8.4 of the Employment Agreement. The sentence also ends in a comma, unfinished.

Releasing the Company of "all of its remaining obligations" on any violation cuts against paragraph 1's carve-out preserving the Employee's claims for amounts due under the Employment Agreement. Which prevails on a minor breach is unresolved.

The heading describes him as "President of International Operations" whereas Section 2.1 gives the titles President of Ajuba India and President-International for Ajuba. The titles are stated inconsistently.

This gives him responsibility for Finance/Accounting/Cash Management across Ajuba US and all subsidiaries, yet Section 8.4(a) provides that consolidating, eliminating or outsourcing exactly those functions is not a material diminution, and Section 2.1 deems the Schedule amended accordingly. The duty and the carve-out pull against each other.

The Schedule has him report to the Chairman of the Board, while Section 2.1 requires him to "report directly to the Board (or selected designee of the Board of Directors of the Parent)" — and Section 2.1 makes the Schedule control over conflicts only with the Bylaws. The reporting line conflicts.

Section 2.2(f) conditions the $200,000 on the Novi office being "restructured", while the Schedule reduces the Employee's task to overseeing termination of the Novi lease. What counts as the restructuring is stated at two different levels.

Section 2.2(f) recites that Schedule I "sets forth the specific cost savings for each action and a reasonable risk assessment", while this paragraph disclaims any representation or warranty as to cost savings or client reaction. The operative bonus condition and the disclaimer point in different directions.

Costs are made "the sole responsibility of Ajuba", yet Section 2.2(f) makes Ajuba India the payor of the Reorganization Bonus and the Agreement defines "Company" as both entities. Which entity bears the closure costs is stated inconsistently with the rest of the package.
